item.title: Why are people more willing to obey justified commands?
item.description: This paper explores the human tendency toward a high reliance on reasons (or justifications), and how this mindset influences our response to commands and requests. Through psychological experiments and real-life cases, it reveals why providing justifications makes ideas more readily accepted.
item.content:encoded:
You must clearly state who will do what, when, where, and why. If you write a note to a subordinate instructing them to do something but fail to explain the reason, Brown might fire you because he is very clear that an idea is most easily accepted only when its reasons are meticulously laid out.

Unfortunately, this tendency to value reasons is so strong that even if the reason provided is meaningless or inaccurate, it can make one’s commands and requests easier to comply with. A psychological experiment has proven this. In this experiment, the researcher successfully cut in front of a long line waiting for a copier, giving the reason: “I need to copy a few things.” This unfortunate side effect of the tendency to value reasons is actually a conditioned reflex. This conditioned reflex occurs because most people believe that things with reasons are important. Naturally, certain businesses and cults often utilize various catchy/sensational reasons to achieve their hidden objectives.

item.title: Deprivation of Hyper-reaction Tendency: Psychological Mechanisms and Real-World Impact
item.description: This paper discusses the 'Deprivation Super-Reaction Tendency' in psychology, analyzing its manifestation and influence in human behavior, ideology, labor-capital relations, gambling, auctions, and investment decisions.
item.content:encoded:
Asymmetry of Pleasure and Pain

The pleasure a person derives from gaining $10 is not equal to the pain caused by losing $10. In other words, the damage caused by loss far exceeds the pleasure brought by gain. Furthermore, if a person is about to receive something they desperately desire, but this item is snatched away at the last moment, their reaction will be as if they had owned it for a long time and it was suddenly taken away.

Examples of the Endowment Super-Reaction Tendency

The Munger couple once owned a gentle and kind dog that exhibited a clear endowment super-reaction tendency. There was only one way to make this dog bite: by snatching the food out of its mouth while feeding it. Once you did this, the friendly dog would immediately bite you; it couldn’t control itself. For the dog, there is nothing more foolish than biting its owner. However, the dog cannot avoid this foolishness because it naturally possesses an automatic loss reaction mechanism. Humans are similar to the Munger family’s dog; when people face the loss or potential loss of property, love, friendship, territory, opportunity, identity, or any other valuable thing, they usually exhibit intense, irrational reactions, even if the loss is minor. Consequently, internal conflicts arising from threatened territory often cause massive damage to the entire organization.

The Impact of the Endowment Super-Reaction Tendency on Ideology

The endowment super-reaction tendency usually helps protect a certain ideology or religious view because it stimulates feelings of aversion or hatred toward public questioners. Part of the reason for this is that these views are already established and possess a strong belief maintenance system, and if the ideas of the questioners spread, they will weaken the influence of the original view. Humanities and Social Sciences departments in universities, law schools, and various business organizations all exhibit this ideology-based group consciousness, almost rejecting any external information that contradicts their knowledge system. If the public critic was once a member of that ideology, the hostility will be even stronger for two reasons: (1) the act of betrayal triggers an additional loss reaction because a “comrade” has been lost; (2) there is a fear that the opponent’s views are more persuasive because they come from a former member.

The Impact of the Endowment Super-Reaction Tendency on Labor-Management Relations

The endowment super-reaction tendency has had a profound impact on labor-management relations. Most of the deaths in labor disputes that occurred before World War I were caused by employers attempting to cut wages. Although fatal conflicts are less common today, more companies have gone bankrupt because fierce market competition leaves only two choices: either reduce wages—which is often difficult to achieve consensus on—or the enterprise goes bankrupt. The loss reaction prompts many workers to resist wage reduction plans, even though accepting the wage cut might be more beneficial to them.

The Endowment Super-Reaction Tendency and Gambling Behavior

The endowment super-reaction tendency is also one of the major reasons why some gamblers lose everything. Firstly, it makes gamblers eager to recover after losing money; the more they lose, the stronger this feeling of dissatisfaction becomes. Secondly, the most addictive forms of gambling often involve scenarios designed as “almost wins,” which trigger a strong loss reaction. Designers of some slot machine programs maliciously exploit this human weakness.

The Endowment Super-Reaction Tendency and Auction Behavior

The endowment super-reaction tendency often causes participants in public auctions to pay high prices. The “social validation” tendency, which we will discuss next, prompts bidders to believe that others’ bids are reasonable, while the loss reaction drives them to bid higher. To avoid paying unreasonable prices at public auctions, the best method is Warren Buffett’s advice: don’t participate in these auctions. The loss reaction, combined with the tendency to avoid inconsistency, often leads to a form of business failure: exhausting all quality assets in order to save a poor investment project.

The Endowment Super-Reaction Tendency and Investment Decisions

Shareholders of Berkshire Hathaway never sell or even gift a single share after the company’s market value has increased significantly. This behavior stems partly from rational calculation, but several psychological factors are also at play: (1) the reward super-reaction; (2) the “status quo bias” caused by the tendency to avoid inconsistency; (3) the “endowment effect” triggered by the tendency toward self-regard.

item.title: Why does the human brain resist changing thoughts?
item.description: This paper explores the human brain's tendency to resist new ideas, analyzes how this psychological mechanism leads to cognitive errors, and why people find it difficult to abandon old concepts.
item.content:encoded:
The brain’s resistance to change also makes people tend to keep the original state of things such as previous conclusions, loyalty, identity, socially recognized roles, and so on.

If the tendency to avoid doubt, combined with the tendency to make quick decisions and refuse to change those decisions, is allowed to combine, it will cause modern people’s cognition to have a large number of errors. And the actual situation is indeed like this. All of us have interacted with many obstinate people—those people who stubbornly hold onto the wrong ideas formed when they were young, refusing to let go even until they enter the grave.

The reason new ideas are difficult to accept is not because they are inherently too complex. New ideas are rejected because they are inconsistent with existing old ideas. Professor Keynes’ implied meaning is: The way the human brain and the human egg operate are very similar. When a sperm enters the egg, the egg automatically activates a sealing mechanism, preventing other sperm from entering. The human brain strongly tends toward the same result. Therefore, people tend to accumulate a large number of rigid conclusions and attitudes, and they do not often check them, let alone change them, even when there is a large amount of evidence showing they are wrong.

item.title: It feels extremely unreliable, the probability of error is extremely high.
item.description: This article explores how humans are easily susceptible to various forms of deception, from magic to perceptual errors in daily life.
item.content:encoded:
Humans are easily deceived, whether by meticulously designed human tricks, accidental environmental factors, or highly effective techniques that people have diligently practiced and mastered. It is easy for people to be fooled. One of the reasons for this outcome is the subtle effect in human perception. If a stimulus is maintained below a certain level, humans will not perceive its existence. Because of this reason, a magician can make the Statue of Liberty disappear after a dramatic flourish in the dark. The audience does not know that they are sitting on a slowly rotating platform. This platform rotates very slowly, so no one can notice it. When the curtain on the platform is drawn back where the Statue of Liberty appeared, it looks like it has vanished.

Some professors like to use experiments to demonstrate the perceptual flaws caused by contrast. They will have students place one hand in a bucket of hot water and the other hand into a bucket of cold water. Then they will suddenly ask the students to place both hands into a bucket of lukewarm water. Although both hands are in the same bucket of water, one hand feels as if it was just placed in cold water, and the other hand feels as if it was just placed in hot water. When people realize that simple contrast alone can easily deceive perception in a place where the thermometer will not be wrong, and that cognition and perception are the same, they will be deceived by simple contrast. Then, they will not only understand how a magician tricks people, but they will also understand how life plays tricks on people. The tendencies within the human perception and cognition system that are generally very useful often make mistakes, and if we do not guard against them carefully, we will easily be manipulated by others.

item.title: The Navy's Rules: Cruel but effective
item.description: This article explores the strict rules and culture within the navy, emphasizing the gravity of responsibility in adverse environments and the potential career termination that failure can bring.
item.content:encoded:
If you are a naval captain who has worked for 24 hours straight and need to go to sleep, so you hand the ship over to a highly capable first mate in harsh conditions, and he runs the ship aground—which clearly isn’t your fault—they won’t send you to a military tribunal, but your naval career is over.

The naval system certainly encourages people to be fully focused in adverse conditions—because they know that if something goes wrong, there will be absolutely no forgiveness.

Napoleon said he preferred luckier generals—he wouldn’t support a defeated commander. Similarly, the Navy prefers luckier captains.

Regardless of why your ship ran aground, your career is over anyway. No one is interested in your mistake (the reason). That is the rule of the Navy—and in every aspect, it is good for everyone.

item.title: If
item.description: Even when others accuse and doubt, by still believing in oneself and facing life's challenges with composure and dignity, one can become a true powerhouse.
item.content:encoded:
If you can remain calm, when the people around you all go mad and accuse you,

If you can believe in yourself, when everyone doubts you—let them doubt.

If you endure waiting, yet are not weary from the wait; or if you suffer deception, yet do not repay it with lies; or if you are met with hatred, yet do not retaliate with hatred—able to remain composed when displeased, and able to avoid flattery…

If you can converse with common folk with courtesy, or walk alongside kings—without becoming subservient;

If both enemies and close friends cannot harm you;

If you care for everyone, yet cannot function if anyone is missing;

If you are thinking of venting your anger, go run for sixty seconds, and the earth and all things upon it will belong to you, And more importantly, you will be a true man, my child!

If you can combine a collection of knowledge patterns and answer after another why, you will be able to think more deeply; by the same token, if you tell people things, always tell them the reason, and they will understand what you say more profoundly, they will value what you say more highly, and they will be more inclined to follow what you say. Even if they do not understand your reasoning, they will be more inclined to listen to your words.

item.title: Life is more than just accumulating wealth smartly.
item.description: This article discusses things in life that are more important than earning money, such as avoiding mistakes, contentment with the status quo, and guarding against jealousy.
item.content:encoded:
Life is not just about shrewdly accumulating wealth.

Most success in life and business comes from knowing what you should avoid: premature death, bad marriages, etc. Avoid contracting AIDS, cutting in front of traffic and trains, and drug use. Cultivate good mental habits.

Avoid wicked people, especially those seductive opposite-sex individuals.

If you are unpopular among those around you because of your uniqueness… then let them be.

Be Content with What You Have

Here is a truth your investment advisor might object to: If you are already quite wealthy, and other people’s wealth is growing faster than yours—for example, by making money on high-risk stocks—so what?! There will always be people whose wealth is growing faster than yours. This is not a tragedy. Soros could not tolerate others making money from the technology industry while he did not, and he lost a ton of money. We simply don’t care (that others made money in the tech industry).

Beware of Envy

Focusing on the idea that others are making money (faster than you) is a fatal sin. Envy is truly a foolish sin because it is a sin from which you cannot derive any pleasure. It will only cause you suffering; it will not bring you any joy. Why are you envious?

item.title: The Importance of Diverse Thinking Models
item.description: Many people absurdly cling to incorrect ideas. Keynes said: "Introducing new ideas is not difficult; the difficult part is clearing out those old ideas."
item.content:encoded:
The Importance of Diverse Thinking Models

You must understand and master the key theories from important disciplines, and you must frequently apply them. You need to utilize all these thinking models, not just rely on a few. Most people focus on only one discipline—for example, economics—and try to solve all problems with a single method. As the saying goes: “The person holding a hammer sees the world as a nail.” This is an inefficient way of thinking.

The Correct Way to Study

If you adopt the learning method that many students use, you will fail to truly master those 100 necessary mental models. Those students study well, but then they give the knowledge back to the professor, and after getting the score, they discard the knowledge, as if pouring water out of a bathtub so they can fill it with new water next time. If this is how you approach learning these 100 thinking models, you will achieve nothing in life. You must take these models seriously and allow them to become abilities that you can call upon at any time.

The Power of Common Sense

Possessing systematic common sense—very fundamental knowledge—is an extremely powerful tool. While computer technology has brought convenience, it has also brought many dangers. People calculate too much, but think too little. Having common sense not only means you can identify wisdom, but it also means you can reject foolishness. When you eliminate many unnecessary distractions, you prevent yourself from falling into chaos.

We read a lot of books. Everyone I know is like that. However, reading alone is not enough:

You must possess a disposition that allows you to understand ideas and make rational decisions. Most people fail to grasp the correct ideas, or they don’t know how to apply them. The richer your foundational knowledge, the less new knowledge you need to absorb.

item.title: Waiting for the wisdom of investment methods and diversified investment
item.description: Exploring the core philosophy of value investing, including the buy-and-hold strategy and the importance of proper diversification, and sharing Berkshire's successful experience.
item.content:encoded:
The Sitting and Waiting Investment Method

If you buy something because its value is undervalued, then when its price rises to your expected level, you must consider selling it. That is difficult. But, if you can buy a few great companies, then you can sit back and relax. That is a good thing. We tend to allocate large sums of money in places where we don’t need to make further decisions.

Diversified Investing

The idea that investment should be as diversified as possible is a crazy notion. We do not believe that highly diversified investments can produce good results. We believe that almost all good investments have relatively low diversification. If you remove our 15 best decisions, our performance would be very mediocre. What you need is not a large amount of action, but extreme patience. You must stick to principles, and when the opportunity comes, you must forcefully grasp it. Over the years, Berkshire has made money by betting on things it is confident about.

item.title: The key to success: patience, learning, and the power of personality
item.description: This article explores the core elements of success, including the importance of patience, the habit of continuous learning, and good personality traits, and cites the wisdom of figures such as Charlie Munger and Benjamin Franklin.
item.content:encoded:
What you need is not a lot of action, but a lot of patience

What you need is not a lot of action, but a lot of patience. You must stick to the principles, and when the opportunity comes, you must grab it with all your might. There are many situations that are worse than being swamped in cash and doing nothing. I remember the time when I lacked cash—I certainly don’t want to go back to that time. ——Charlie Munger

Money is something with extremely powerful reproductive power

This is the stone that can turn all your lead into gold… Remember, money is something with extremely powerful reproductive power. Money gives birth to money, and that money gives birth to even more money. ——Benjamin Franklin

Cultivating Curiosity and the Habit of Continuous Learning

If you want to become smart, the question you must constantly ask is “Why, why, why.” Cultivate yourself into a lifelong learner through extensive reading; cultivate curiosity, and strive to become a little bit smarter every day.

Humility: Acknowledging your ignorance is the beginning of wisdom

  1. Operate only within your clearly defined circle of competence
  2. Identify and verify negative evidence
  3. Resist the desire for false precision and erroneous certainty

Patience: Restraining humanity’s innate preference for action

  1. “Compounding is the eighth wonder of the world” (Einstein), don’t interrupt it unless necessary
  2. Avoid unnecessary transaction taxes and friction costs; never act just for the sake of action
  3. Stay clear-headed when luck comes
  4. Enjoy the results, and enjoy the process, because you are living in the process

The key to success lies in character and learning ability

“Why are some people smarter than others? This has partly to do with innate character. Some people’s characters are not suitable for investing. They are always restless, or always worried. But if you possess a good character—and here, primarily meaning you are very patient and can proactively act when you know you should—then you can gradually understand this game through practice and learning.

Evidently, the wider the sources from which you draw lessons, rather than just from your own bad experiences, the better you will become. I haven’t found anyone who can do this quickly. As an investor, Warren Buffett is much better than when I first met him, and I am the same. If we stagnate at a certain stage, satisfied with the knowledge we already possess, our performance will be much worse than it is now.

So the trick is continuous learning, and I don’t believe that those who don’t enjoy the learning process can continue to learn.”

item.title: Munger's 100 Mental Models
item.description: A compilation of 100 mental models recommended by Charlie Munger, covering fields such as mathematics, economics, psychology, and physics, used for solving complex problems more effectively.
item.content:encoded:
I. Mathematics and Logic

  1. Compound Interest Principle
  2. Probability Theory (Fermat-Pascal System)
  3. Permutations and Combinations
  4. Decision Tree Analysis
  5. Bayes’ Theorem
  6. Expected Value Calculation
  7. Random Walk Theory
  8. Game Theory
  9. Linear Regression
  10. Nonlinear System
  11. Critical Mass (Phase Transition Point)
  12. Power Law Distribution (Heavy-Tail Theory)
  13. Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)
  14. Butterfly Effect
  15. Fractal Geometry

II. Microeconomics and Business

  1. Opportunity Cost
  2. Economies of Scale
  3. Moat (Competitive Advantage)
  4. Sunk Cost Fallacy
  5. Substitution Effect
  6. Diminishing Marginal Utility
  7. Supply and Demand Relationship
  8. Price Elasticity
  9. Agency Cost
  10. Information Asymmetry
  11. Network Effect
  12. Flywheel Effect
  13. Two-Sided Market
  14. Anchoring Effect
  15. Cost Shifting (or Cost Transfer)

III. Psychology and Behavioral Science

  1. Confirmation Bias
  2. Loss Aversion
  3. Availability Bias
  4. Overconfidence Effect
  5. Herd Mentality (or Conformity)
  6. Social Identity
  7. Self-Serving Bias
  8. Hindsight Bias
  9. Mental Accounting
  10. Selective Attention
  11. Emotional Hijacking
  12. Contrast Effect
  13. Authority Bias
  14. Fear-Based Decision Making
  15. Pleasure-Pain Principle
  16. Cognitive Dissonance
  17. Attribution Bias
  18. Illusion of Control
  19. Adaptive Preference
  20. Decision Fatigue

IV. Physics and Engineering

  1. Redundant Backup System
  2. Fracture Point Theory
  3. Law of Conservation of Energy
  4. Second Law of Thermodynamics (Entropy Increase)
  5. Tension and Stress Equilibrium
  6. Feedback Loop (Positive/Negative)
  7. System Stability
  8. Modular Design
  9. Fault Tree Analysis
  10. Safety Margin (Engineering)

V. Biology and Evolution

  1. Survival of the Fittest
  2. Genetic Competition
  3. Niche Theory (Ecological Niche Theory)
  4. Co-evolution
  5. Mutation and Selection
  6. Population Dynamics
  7. Metabolic Efficiency
  8. Principles of the Immune System
  9. Viral Transmission (or Viral Spread)
  10. Principle of Competitive Exclusion

VI. Statistics and Data Analysis

  1. Central Limit Theorem
  2. Law of Large Numbers
  3. Regression Mean
  4. Sample Bias
  5. Correlation $\neq$ Causation
  6. Data Visualization Trap
  7. Spurious Correlation
  8. Significance Testing
  9. Data Overfitting
  10. Confounding Variable (or Confounder)

VII. Philosophy and Cognitive Science

  1. First Principles
  2. Inversion Thinking (or Thinking in Reverse)
  3. Occam’s Razor
  4. Black Swan Theory
  5. Falsifiability (Popper)
  6. Knowledge Transfer
  7. Metacognition
  8. Cognitive Load Theory
  9. Dual System Thinking (Fast/Slow Thinking)
  10. Humility Hypothesis

VIII. Sociology and History

  1. Cultural Inertia
  2. Institutional Path Dependence
  3. Revolutionary Cycle Theory
  4. Technology Diffusion Curve
  5. Historical Recurrence (or Historical Repetition)
  6. Group Polarization
  7. Paradox of Power Concentration
  8. Interest Group Dynamics (or Interest Group Game)
  9. Laws of Civilizational Rise and Fall
  10. Unintended Consequences

Usage Instructions:

  1. Dynamic Update: In practical application, the model must be expanded according to new fields (such as AI, Quantum Computing).
  2. Cross-Validation: For the same problem, multiple disciplines must be called upon (e.g., investment decisions require combining Compound Interest, Psychological Biases, and Moats).
  3. Weight Adjustment: The importance of the model varies depending on the scenario (e.g., medical decisions emphasize probability, political negotiations emphasize Game Theory).

These models do not exist in isolation; Munger emphasizes solving complex problems through the “Lollapalooza Effect” (the exponential effect generated by the superposition of multiple models). For example:

  • Tesla Valuation = Compound Growth + Network Effect + Behavioral Economics (Social Identity) + Policy Driver (Subsidy Leverage).

item.title: Investment equals going out to bet on horses
item.description: You are looking for bets with mispriced odds. That is the essence of investing.
item.content:encoded: “Investing is like horse gambling. We must look for a horse whose probability of winning is one-half, and whose odds are one-to-three. What you are looking for is a wager with mispriced odds. This is the essence of investing. You must possess enough knowledge to know whether the odds of the wager are mispriced. This is value investing.”

item.title: Poor Charlie's Guide & Long-termism
item.description: In-depth exploration of how to overcome the limitations of Graham value investing, focusing on high-quality companies, seizing investment opportunities, and the impact of taxation on investment returns.
item.content:encoded:
We were initially believers in Graham, and we achieved some success through that method. But as time went on, our investment eye became sharper.

Breaking Graham’s Limitations

We found that some stocks, even if priced at two or three times their book value, were still very cheap. This is because these companies possess unique market positions and hold the potential for sustained growth. Perhaps a company’s management is exceptionally good, or perhaps the entire management system is outstanding. By breaking Graham’s limitations and employing some quantitative methods that might make Graham uneasy to find undervalued stocks, we began to focus on higher-quality enterprises.

The Value of Quality Companies

It is worth mentioning that the vast majority of Berkshire Hathaway’s hundreds of billions of dollars in assets come from these high-quality companies. The initial two or three hundred million dollars were acquired by searching around, much like using a Geiger counter. But the vast majority of wealth comes from investing in those great companies.

Grasping Opportunities Precisely

Instead of pretending that you understand everything, it is better to seize a few opportunities that you are certain about. If you choose to do what is feasible from the start, rather than doing what is infeasible, your chances of success will greatly increase. Isn’t that obvious?

Investing in Corporate Quality, Not Management

Betting on the quality of the company is more prudent than betting on the quality of the management. In other words, if a choice must be made, one should place more weight on the company’s growth prospects than on the manager’s wisdom.

The Impact of Taxation

Let’s talk about the impact of taxation. Suppose you make an investment for 30 years with an average compound annual growth rate of 15%, and you ultimately pay a 35% income tax. In this scenario, your after-tax average compound annual growth rate will drop to 13.3%.

The Impact of Tax Burden on Returns

Conversely, if you invest in the same project, but pay 35% income tax every year after achieving a 15% return, your compound return rate will become 15% minus 35% of 15%, which is 9.75% annually (15% - 15% × 35% = 9.75%). The difference in returns between these two scenarios exceeds 3.5%. For a 30-year investment, the profit generated by an extra 3.5% return each year will absolutely surprise you. If you can hold the stocks of great companies for the long term, the savings from lower income tax alone can add a massive amount of wealth for you.

item.title: The key to earning big money is not in buying and selling, but in waiting.
item.description: Exploring the philosophy of patience in investing, integrating the investment principles of Jesse Livermore, Charlie Munger, and Warren Buffett, and emphasizing the importance of waiting and long-term holding.
item.content:encoded:
Patience: The Art of Patient Waiting

Look at those hedge funds—do you think they know how to wait? They fundamentally don’t know how to wait! In my personal portfolio, I have held U.S. Treasuries or municipal bonds ranging from $10 million to $12 million for several consecutive years, and then I just stopped touching them, just quietly waiting, waiting…

“As Jesse Livermore said: ‘The secret to making big money is not in buying and selling… but in waiting.’”

Charlie’s Principles and Investment Philosophy

Charlie believes that forethought, patience, self-discipline, and impartiality are the most fundamental guiding principles. No matter how the outside world views things, and no matter how my own emotions fluctuate, he always adheres to these principles. Although many people believe that “one must learn to adapt to random circumstances,” Charlie remains unshaken. If one can firmly adhere to these principles, they can demonstrate one of Munger’s most famous traits: infrequent trading.

Like Buffett, Munger believes that just a few decisions are enough to achieve a successful investment career. Therefore, when Charlie identifies a company he likes, he makes a very large bet, and usually holds the stock of that company for the long term (see “The Investment Performance of Charlie Munger’s Partnership” in Chapter One). Charlie calls this method the “Sit-and-Wait Investment Strategy” (or “Patient Waiting Method”) and clearly points out its advantages: “You pay less in fees to the trader, and you hear less nonsense; if this method works, the tax system will give you an extra 1% to 3% return every year.” In his view, buying just three stocks is enough. Therefore, Charlie is willing to commit a large proportion of capital to individual “watched” opportunities. No Wall Street institution, financial advisor, or open-end fund manager makes such a declaration!

Lessons from Warren’s Investment Course

“When Warren was in business school, he said: ‘I can improve your final financial situation with just one attendance card; this card has 20 slots, so you only have 20 chances to punch in throughout your life—this represents the number of times you can invest in your life. Once you punch the card, you can’t invest anymore. Under this rule, you will truly consider every investment action; you will have to put large sums of money into the projects you truly want to invest in. This way, your performance will be much better.’”

The Rhythm and Strategy of Investing

Quickly eliminate what should not be done, then launch a skilled, interdisciplinary attack on what should be done, and then, when the right opportunity comes—only when the right opportunity comes—act decisively.

item.title: Every day, there is a lot of information misleading you.
item.description: This article narrates the story of how Britain, during WWII, falsely claimed that pilots consumed large amounts of carrots to gain extraordinary night vision capabilities, thereby concealing its night radar technology.
item.content:encoded:
During WWII, Britain possessed radar capable of night targeting, but they didn’t want the Germans to find out. So, they claimed that their pilots gained extraordinary night vision because they ate a lot of carrots. The grand principles you encounter are basically teaching you to eat carrots.

Open-ended funds charge 2% in fees annually, and then those brokers make people switch back and forth between different funds, adding another 3% to 4% in fees. Poor ordinary fund holders hand over their money to professionals, only to receive terrible results. I find this disgusting. When people buy your product, you should be making their assets grow. But in this country, fund managers only care about making money for themselves. This industry is ridiculous because, looking at the net returns, the entire investment management industry, when combined, hasn’t provided added value to all the clients’ assets. This is how the industry operates.
